question: How can existing LLM-based agents be organised in one framework, drawing on production systems and cognitive architectures, and what does it suggest for building future agents?
hypothesis: Control structures from cognitive architectures used with production systems are equally applicable to turning LLMs into language agents.
contributions: CoALA: a conceptual framework with modular memory, a structured internal/external action space and a generalized decision loop
A retrospective survey casting recent agents (SayCan, ReAct, Voyager, Generative Agents, Tree of Thoughts) into the framework
Prospective actionable directions and open conceptual questions

limits: Conceptual framework: no experiments, no benchmarks, no measured numbers of its own.
Case studies are retrospective redescriptions of published agents, not evidence the framework predicts performance.
Authors concede the framework may need changing as LLMs scale (GPT-N thought experiment) and that boundary questions (internal vs external) are conceptual.
Written in 2023: does not cover later tool-use APIs, MCP, or reasoning models.
practices: Structure agents modularly rather than monolithically (Sec 6).
Design in order: choose memory modules, define internal action read/write access, then the decision procedure (Sec 6, retail assistant example).
Give episodic memory read/write but semantic and procedural read-only for a retail assistant (Sec 6).
Prefer minimal action space; treat learning and grounding actions as safety-relevant (Sec 6).
Use structured prompting frameworks and output parsing to update working-memory variables (Sec 6).
Treat learning as a choosable action in the decision cycle, deferrable (Sec 7).
Add metareasoning: fix search budgets knowingly, or route between decision sub-procedures (Sec 6).
